extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and prosecuting attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and drafting rejections under AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) during patent examination, including required factual inquiries, use of AIA prior art rules, exceptions, form paragraphs, and procedures for overcoming rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of Obviousness Determination (effective filing date)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 determines obviousness before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, rather than as of the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 practice where the Office used effective filing date as a proxy for invention date unless earlier invention date was established (e.g., by affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131). As a practical matter, this distinction affects cases only when pre-AIA 103 is applicable and there is evidence of an invention date prior to the effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of 'differences between the claimed invention and the prior art'
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 103 requires consideration of 'the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language does not change the approach to obviousness determinations: claims are the measure of the invention. The MPEP notes that the Court has equated 'the subject matter sought to be patented' with the claims (Graham v. John Deere). Examiners should ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue when formulating an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of invention is irrelevant to patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory language: 'Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying 35 U.S.C. 103, examiners should not base patentability determinations on how the inventor arrived at the invention; focus is on the claimed invention vs prior art as of the effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 prior art for 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If a document qualifies as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or (a)(2), and is not subject to an exception under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), it may be applied in a rejection under AIA 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should determine whether a reference is prior art under AIA 102 before relying on it for an obviousness rejection. See Hazeltine Res., Inc. v. Brenner for the principle that previously filed applications can constitute prior art. If a reference is excepted under 102(b) it may not be used for purposes that require prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-enabling disclosures are prior art for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-enabling disclosure is prior art for all it teaches for purposes of determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a reference does not enable practice of the invention (and thus may not anticipate under 102), it still may be relied upon for what it teaches when supporting an obviousness rejection (citing Symbol Techs. Inc. v. Opticon Inc.; Beckman Instruments v. LKB Produkter AB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for Obviousness — Factual Inquiries (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual inquiries summarized for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are: (1) determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This four-part test (the 'Graham factors') should be the basis for the factual background of any obviousness determination. Examiners must apply these inquiries and may use form paragraph ¶ 7.23.aia when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating and supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 must be supported by an explanation (rationale) showing why the claimed invention would have been obvious, following MPEP § 2144 and related guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should provide an explanation of the rejection (how the references map to the claim limitations and why one of ordinary skill would be motivated to combine or modify references with a reasonable expectation of success). See MPEP § 2144 for guidance on appropriate rationales (implicit disclosure, reliance on scientific theory, common knowledge, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prescribed form paragraphs in Office Actions for 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPEP provides specific form paragraphs for use in making rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (e.g., ¶ 7.06, ¶ 7.20.aia, ¶ 7.21.aia, ¶ 7.22.aia, ¶ 7.27.aia, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Examiner Notes for each form paragraph regarding when each should be used (e.g., 7.06 must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in certain transitional applications; 7.20.aia quotes the statute and must be preceded by 7.03.aia; many paragraphs should be used only once per action and in a particular order). Include the required explanatory material after the form paragraph as directed (see cross-references to relevant MPEP sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and limits of prior art exceptions under AIA 102(b)(2)(C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA, common ownership, obligation to assign, or joint research agreement must exist on or before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to except a disclosure from being prior art under 102(a)(2). When an exception applies under AIA 102(b)(2)(C), a reference is not prior art at all and may not be applied in anticipation or an obviousness rejection or as a secondary reference in non-statutory double patenting rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the exception applies, the reference may not be used for any purpose requiring prior art; however, claims of such disclosures could still be the basis for statutory double patenting or non-statutory double patenting rejections. Compare to pre-AIA 103(c), which operated differently; ensure the statement of common ownership or required disclosures are timely and in a conspicuous manner per MPEP § 2154.02(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures when applicant attempts to except subject matter under 102(b)(2)(C)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant attempts to show that subject matter disclosed in a reference is excepted under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) (common ownership/assignment/joint research agreement), the submission must include the required statements and amendments (e.g., conspicuous statement of common ownership, amendment to specification to include names for joint research agreements) or the attempt is ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the required statement is not provided, the reference is not excepted and a 102(a)(2) prior art rejection may stand. The MPEP cross-references 37 CFR 1.71(g)(1), 1.104(c)(4)(ii) and gives form paragraphs (e.g., ¶ 7.20.04.aia, ¶ 7.20.05.aia) to explain the deficiency and the required corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventors and presumption of common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application currently names joint inventors, the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered were effectively filed absent evidence to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and effective filing dates for claims not commonly owned so the examiner can consider applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C). Use ¶ 7.20.02.aia in all applications with joint inventors unless claims are clearly restricted to a single claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejections based on copending applications (102(a)(2) prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 may be made based upon a copending application that would constitute prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) if published or patented, using a presumption of future publication or patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such provisional rejections (¶ 7.21.01.aia) should be used when the copending application has a common assignee, common applicant, or at least one common (joint) inventor. Examiner must explain the basis of obviousness and indicate ways the provisional rejection might be overcome (37 CFR 1.130(a)/(b) showings or a §102(b)(2)(C) statement). If the claimed invention is fully disclosed in the copending application, use ¶ 7.15.01.aia instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming AIA prior art rejections via 37 CFR 1.130 showings
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may overcome certain AIA prior art rejections by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the subject matter disclosed was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor (so not prior art under 102(b)(1)(A)); or (2) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure by the inventor or joint inventor (102(b)(1)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural remedies are specifically noted in form paragraphs (e.g., ¶ 7.20.01.aia, ¶ 7.21.01.aia, ¶ 7.21.02.aia) as ways applicants may rebut or overcome rejections that rely on disclosures that might otherwise be excepted from being prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use a combined 102/103 rejection (¶ 7.27.aia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) or, in the alternative, under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) when appropriate; ¶ 7.27.aia enumerates example circumstances where such paragraph may be used rather than separate rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: disputed claim interpretation (one interpretation leads to 102, another to 103); when reference discloses all limitations except a property or function and examiner cannot determine inherent properties but has basis for shifting burden (In re Fitzgerald); genus-species situations where genus disclosure makes a species obvious; product-by-process equivalence questions; means-plus-function equivalence uncertainty; overlapping ranges where reference and claim ranges overlap but reference lacks specific example. Examiners should otherwise make a single rejection under either 102 or 103 whenever possible and must provide full explanation for both alternatives when using ¶ 7.27.aia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining references for a 103 rejection (¶ 7.22.aia and supporting guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over a reference as applied to an earlier claim and further in view of another reference, the examiner must precede ¶ 7.22.aia with ¶ 7.21.aia and provide an explanation of the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must explain how the references are combined and why a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine them with a reasonable expectation of success. Cross-reference to MPEP § 2144 for guidance on appropriate rationales and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: General continuity of pre-AIA obviousness principles under the AIA
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally speaking, and with specified exceptions, pre-AIA notions of obviousness continue to apply under the AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although statutory language and structures changed (e.g., timing, certain exceptions), the substantive legal and analytical framework for obviousness largely remains — apply established case law and MPEP guidance unless the AIA provides a specific change or exception.
